extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, journal editors, and research-integrity observers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing publisher and editorial policies/practices that affect journal quality, editorial independence, and research integrity, especially in the context of commercial academic publishers. Includes evaluation of metrics, business models, editorial workflows, and recruitment of editorial leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of quantity versus quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher documentation or incentives should not emphasize quantity of papers published over their quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors wrote that the documentation 'appeared to emphasize quantity over quality of the papers submitted' and that this perception 'increas[ed]–in our perception–risks of proliferation of poor-quality science.' Use this criterion to flag policies or metrics that could encourage publishing more articles at the expense of selectivity and rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of growth in submissions and published articles as performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance metrics that prioritize 'growth in submissions' and 'growth in published articles' are indicators that volume may be driving strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece quotes Wiley: its performance metrics are 'growth in submissions' and 'growth in published articles' and that 'it’s all driven by volume ultimately.' Evaluate whether such metrics create perverse incentives that could undermine peer review stringency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-access pay-to-publish (APC) business model influence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a journal offers open access via author fees (APCs), that business model should not create pressure to accept more papers for revenue reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes an open access option with an APC of more than $4,000 per article and describes Wiley as having an 'Open Access ("pay to publish") business model.' Assess risks that APCs could bias editorial decisions and whether safeguards exist to separate revenue from editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cascade strategy for redirected submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher strategies that 'cascade' initially rejected articles to other titles in the portfolio should be evaluated for impact on standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley's 'Cascade strategy of finding initially rejected articles another more appropriate home within Wiley’s portfolio' is quoted. Consider whether cascade pathways maintain appropriate review standards or merely relocate lower-quality papers within a publisher's ecosystem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targets or goals to increase publication output
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting numerical goals (e.g., increase publication output by a percentage) should be examined for whether they are goals or coercive requirements and for their real-world impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley proposed 'increasing publication output by 4% over the prior year as a goal rather than a requirement,' which amounted to two additional articles per year in absolute terms. Evaluate clarity (goal vs requirement), proportionality, and potential pressure on editors/reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence between publisher policies and editorial standards / editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher policies and non-negotiable documentation should be coherent with the standards and expectations of editors-in-chief and managing editors; editors need meaningful input and independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors stated they 'no longer believed that the corporate policies and practices of the Journal’s publisher... were coherent with ours.' Use this criterion to assess whether editors have sufficient negotiating power, clarity of roles, and protection of editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes to safeguard research integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers must bolster processes and workflows specifically aimed at safeguarding research integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley said it is 'bolstering processes to safeguard research integrity' and updating editorial/production processes. Evaluate concrete measures (e.g., plagiarism checks, fraud screening, transparent corrections/retractions policies) and whether they are adequate and implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder-aligned editorial and production workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Workflows should meet the needs of authors, librarians, funders, and the academic community, not just business objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley asserts it updates processes to 'improve the author experience' and ensure 'workflows meet the needs of authors, librarians and funders.' Assess whether workflow changes balance these stakeholders and preserve rigorous peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent process for recruiting new editorial leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruitment of new editors should be transparent, advertised, and draw from the wider field to maintain community trust and legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley stated: 'We are currently working with members of the board and wider community to recruit new leadership... This is a fully transparent process that includes advertising and recruiting within the wider field.' Use transparency, community involvement, and advertised searches as markers of good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of best-practice editorial workflows and appropriate scope broadening
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoming editorial teams should introduce best-practice workflows and consider scope adjustments to reflect new and emerging fields while maintaining quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley plans, 'in partnership with the new editorial team, we plan to introduce best practice editorial workflows and broaden the journal’s scope to reflect new and emerging fields.' Evaluate proposed workflow standards and whether scope changes are justified by expertise and safeguards to uphold rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of editors, reviewers, and staff
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal needs qualified and competent editors, reviewers, and staff; lack of competence can lead to fraud, poor review, and low quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and the article point to Wiley/Hindawi struggles with 'lack of good editors, good reviewers, and good staff' and that 'Lots and lots of incompetent people' create an ecosystem where quality work is not supported. Assess recruitment, training, oversight, and accountability measures for editorial teams and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor involvement and buy-in when implementing changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should be involved in and generally supportive of major changes to editorial processes; publishers should seek common ground and compromise with editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley said 'Editors are key to making these changes happen, and our goal is always to reach common ground on changes that support the long-term success of the journal.' Evaluate the degree of consultation, negotiation, and whether changes respect editorial judgment; recognize that mutual parting may be appropriate when compromise is impossible.
